h1: The 8 Best Immersion Blenders Under $50 in 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Immersion Blender Under $50: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 hand blenders under $50 scored on motor, speed control, attachments and build, from basic sticks to 7-in-1 kits.
summary: The Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 is the best immersion blender under $50, thanks to a 500W motor, 12 speeds and a smart blade guard. The KOIOS 5-in-1 is the best value set, the Levstek is the biggest kit, and the MasterChef is the best plain stick with a speed dial.
intro: Shoppers compare immersion blenders by wattage, and that number is the least reliable one on the box. A 1200 watt claim usually means peak power for a moment, not sustained work, and the sticks that last are the ones with a decent shaft, a blade guard and a motor that is allowed to rest. In this price range the real differences are speed control, blade guard design, overheat protection and which accessories come in the box.

We ranked eight hand blenders by those factors. Three list in the $30 to $50 band and four sit under $30, and one has a broad $25 to $50 window. Every pick is a corded stainless steel stick with a detachable shaft, and the question is what you get beyond that. Specs come from the listings, and we do not claim to have blended with them.

Cheap sticks fail in familiar ways. Plastic gearboxes strip when pushed through frozen fruit, motors overheat if run past a minute, open blades splash hot soup, and the shaft can stain with tomato or turmeric. We weighted these points, and we say clearly when a claim is a peak figure.

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 Immersion Blender, 500W, 12 Speeds and Turbo
products.verdict: A 500W blender stick with a whisk, a 24 ounce beaker and a 17 ounce chopper bowl.
products.description:
The Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 pairs a 500 watt high-torque motor with 12 speeds and a Turbo button, and ships with a whisk, a 24 ounce mixing beaker and a 17 ounce food chopper bowl. The blade has a semi-enclosed guard meant to cut splashing and stop food from sticking, the body is scratch-resistant stainless steel, and the listing describes attachments that click on and off. It measures about 17 inches in its longest dimension.

It ranks first because the combination of a mid-range 500 watt motor, a wide speed range and a useful accessory kit beats the stripped-down two-speed sticks at the same shelf price. The guard is a real design feature, since an open blade throws puree against the wall. It beats the KOIOS on guard design, and trades away the KOIOS's extra wattage and lower price.

Buy it if you want to puree soups in the pot, whisk cream and chop onions with one tool. It lists in the $30 to $50 band, the top of the budget. The caveat is that the listing says the motor body, whisk head and any grinder head must stay out of the dishwasher, so wipe those by hand.
cons: Sits at the top of the budget
products.idealFor: Home cooks who want soups, sauces and small chopping jobs from one kit.
products.skipIf: You only want a bare stick.

products.name: KOIOS 5-in-1 Immersion Blender, 1000W, 12 Speeds and Turbo
products.verdict: A five-piece set with a copper motor, overheat protection and a 304 stainless shaft.
products.description:
KOIOS sells a five-piece set that replaces a blender, chopper, whisk, frother and beaker. The listing credits an all-copper motor rated at 1000 watts, twelve speeds plus a turbo boost, and an anti-splash 304 stainless steel shaft that fits most pots, mason jars and wide-mouth cups. Overheat protection is listed, and attachments release with one click.

It ranks second because the shaft material and thermal protection matter more than headline wattage, and under $30 this set offers more in the box than the Bonsenkitchen. It loses on the guard design and on slightly less documentation of accessory sizes. It beats the Levstek on price while giving up some accessory volume and its 20 speeds.

Buy it for hot soups, smoothies and sauces in a small kitchen. It lists under $30. The caveat comes from the listing itself: avoid running it longer than about 60 seconds at a time, and do not blend ice cubes or whole hard spices, since these shorten blade and motor life.
products.idealFor: Small kitchens, dorms and RVs that need one compact tool.

products.name: Levstek 7-in-1 Immersion Blender, 1200W, 20 Speeds
products.verdict: A seven-piece kit with four blades, 20 speeds and generous beakers and cups.
products.description:
The Levstek 7-in-1 lists a pure copper motor at 1200 watts peak, 20 speeds, four stainless steel blades under a splash guard, and a seven-piece set that includes a 700 ml spill-proof beaker, a whisk, a milk frother and a chopper with a 500 ml lower cup and a 200 ml upper cup. Dimensions are around 10.7 by 5.3 by 9.3 inches.

It ranks third because it has the widest accessory range and the most speed steps in the guide, but a big kit means more parts to store and clean. It beats the MasterChef on versatility and loses to the top two on price clarity, as it lists in the $30 to $50 band. The two cup sizes let you mince meat in the larger one and garlic in the smaller one.

Buy it for family cooking, froth and batters. The caveat is the peak wattage figure: peak is not sustained power, so give the motor rests.

products.idealFor: Families who chop, whisk and froth as well as blend.

products.name: MasterChef 400W Stainless Steel Immersion Blender
products.verdict: A 400W stick with variable speed and a dishwasher-safe blending leg.
products.description:
The MasterChef is a licensed product with a 400 watt motor, stainless steel blades and variable speed control. The blending leg detaches and is listed as dishwasher-safe, while the electronic part must only be wiped with a damp cloth. The listing describes use for smoothies, soups, baby food and baking mixes.

It ranks fourth because a speed dial is more useful than a two-button design when you want to control texture, and 400 watts is enough for soups and smoothies. It beats the Turelar 400W on speed control, since it is variable and the Turelar has two steps, but it loses to the kits on accessories.

Buy it if you only want a stick. It lists under $30. The caveat is that it comes with no beaker or chopper, so you will use your own container.
products.idealFor: Shoppers who want a plain stick with a speed dial.
products.skipIf: You want a chopper or whisk.

products.name: Turelar 400W Immersion Blender with Turbo Mode
products.verdict: A 400W stick with pulse sensing, two speeds and a turbo boost.
products.description:
Turelar's 400 watt model uses a copper motor, a pulse-activated sensor, two speeds and a turbo mode. The listing says the shaft is food-grade stainless steel and BPA-free, the blades are a two-prong design that avoids trapping stem fiber, the grip is non-slip, and a hanging ring lets you store it. It measures about 2.5 by 8.5 by 5 inches.

It ranks fifth because two speeds and a turbo are enough for most pots and cups, but there is less control than the MasterChef dial or the 12-speed kits. It beats the OVENTE for extra turbo and slightly stronger motor, and loses to the MasterChef on fine control. The slim shaft fits most bowls, pots and beakers.

Buy it for quick everyday tasks. It lists under $30. The caveat is that the blades are very sharp, so unplug it before you remove or clean any attachment.
products.idealFor: Light jobs like baby food, sauces and soups.
products.skipIf: You blend thick or frozen mixes.

products.name: OVENTE HS560B 300W Immersion Hand Blender
products.verdict: A 300W two-speed blender stick with a one-year limited warranty.
products.description:
The OVENTE HS560B is a 300 watt hand blender with a pulse-activated sensor, low and high speeds, and a slim stainless steel shaft. The listing says the shaft detaches and is dishwasher-safe, the handle is non-slip, and a one-year limited warranty is supported by US-based customer service.

It ranks sixth because 300 watts and two speeds are enough for sauces and smoothies but little more, and it is one of the lowest-power sticks here. It beats the Bonsenkitchen 300W on warranty clarity. The unit is about 14.7 inches long, which suits deep pots.

Buy it for occasional use with some support behind it. It lists under $30. The caveat is low power, so cut food into small pieces and add liquid.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want warranty backing on a basic stick.

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 300W Immersion Hand Blender
products.verdict: A 300W blender stick with one-touch speed buttons and detachable parts.
products.description:
The Bonsenkitchen 300W is an electric handheld blender with a 300 watt motor, two speed buttons and sharp blades. The listing says the blades are dishwasher-safe but the body must never be immersed in water or put through a dishwasher, and it advises pausing every 20 to 30 seconds for tough ingredients, avoiding ice and frozen fruit without liquid, and removing stones from fruit.

It ranks seventh because the usage limits are frank, which helps set expectations, but power is modest. It beats nothing above it on features, and trades power for price. The dimensions are around 5.5 by 9.3 by 2.6 inches.

Buy it for smoothies, purees and marinades in small batches. It lists under $30. The caveat is the overheat risk, so follow the pause rule.
products.idealFor: Light blending of sauces and baby food.

products.name: Turelar 1100W 5-in-1 Immersion Blender Set
products.verdict: A 1100W five-piece set with limited published detail.
products.description:
Turelar's 5-in-1 set is advertised with an 1100 watt motor and a bundle of accessories. The listing gives little else to confirm, such as speed steps, container sizes or warranty terms, and the price band spans $25 to $50.

It ranks last because a big wattage number without supporting specs is a weak argument. It beats nothing here on documentation, but if the set matches the claim it could compete with the KOIOS. Wattage on small blenders is often a peak figure.

Buy it only if the current price is low and the accessories fit your needs. The caveat is that missing details mean you should check the listing for container sizes before you order.
products.idealFor: Shoppers who want a bundle and accept limited detail.

methodology.title: Motor and real power
methodology.description: We treated wattage as a peak claim, and looked for copper windings, overheat protection and stated run-time limits.

methodology.title: Speed control
methodology.description: A dial or 12 to 20 speeds, pulse and turbo were compared with two-button designs, since texture control needs steps.

methodology.title: Blade guard and shaft
methodology.description: Semi-enclosed guards, 304 stainless steel and shaft length were weighed for splash control and pot depth.

methodology.title: Attachments
methodology.description: Beakers, choppers, whisks and frothers were credited where the listing gives sizes and fit.

methodology.title: Cleanup and value
methodology.description: Dishwasher-safe parts, warranty terms and price bands were weighed against what is in the box.

whatMatters.detail: Wattage on small appliances is usually a peak rating, so a 1000 watt label does not mean sustained power. Copper windings, overheat protection and a stated run time, such as no more than 60 seconds at a time, say more about durability than the number. Check whether the listing says copper motor, overheat protection or a run-time limit.

A variable dial or 12 to 20 speeds lets you start slow to avoid splashing and finish fast for smooth purees. Two-speed models work but give less control, and a pulse button helps on thick mixes. Check how many speeds are listed, and whether Turbo is a momentary button.

A bell-shaped or semi-enclosed guard keeps the blade from splashing and protects non-stick pots from scratches. A 304 stainless steel shaft resists staining and corrosion from tomato and acidic foods. Look for the guard design, the shaft material and the shaft length, since deep pots need a longer stick.

A beaker, chopper and whisk turn one motor into several tools, but only if the sizes suit your cooking. A 17 ounce chopper handles an onion, while a 500 ml cup handles a batch of mince. Check the container capacities on the listing, and make sure the beaker is tall and narrow enough for the blade.

Detachable shafts are easy to rinse or put in the dishwasher, but the motor body must be wiped by hand. A written warranty is a better sign than slogans. Check which parts are dishwasher-safe and whether a warranty term is stated.

faq.q: Can I use these in a non-stick pot?
faq.a: The KOIOS listing says its shaft is safe for non-stick pots, and guarded designs like the Bonsenkitchen reduce scratching. Keep the blade off the pot bottom, and lift gently to avoid contact.
Lifting the blender out of the liquid while it runs. Always switch it off, wait for the blade to stop and keep the blade submerged during use, because splashing hot soup is the most common injury.

faq.q: Is the Bonsenkitchen worth it over the KOIOS?
faq.a: If you want a splash guard and a chopper bowl, yes, though it lists in a higher price band. If you want the lowest price and an overheat-protected motor, the KOIOS is the better value.

faq.q: How do I blend frozen fruit?
faq.a: Add enough liquid, cut fruit into small pieces and pulse in short bursts. The listings advise against ice cubes and whole spices on several models, and to pause every 20 to 30 seconds.

faq.q: How do I clean an immersion blender?
faq.a: Rinse the shaft right after use, or run it in a tall cup of warm soapy water for a few seconds. Never submerge the motor body, and let parts air-dry before you store them.

faq.q: Do these work for whipping cream?
faq.a: Models with a whisk attachment, such as the Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1, KOIOS and Levstek, can do it. A bare stick will not whip cream well.

finalTake: The Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 is the best immersion blender under $50 for most kitchens, with a sensible 500 watt motor, 12 speeds and a splash guard. The KOIOS is the value pick for a small kitchen, and the Levstek is the biggest kit. Treat any wattage number as a peak claim, and never run a cheap stick for more than a minute at a time.
